text: Abul Kalam Ghulam Muhiyuddin (11 November 1888 – 22 February 1958), widely known as Maulana Azad and sometimes referred to as Abul Kalam Azad, was an Indian writer, activist in the Indian independence movement, and statesman. A senior leader of the Indian National Congress, he became the first Minister of Education in the independent Indian government, and his contributions to establishing India’s education foundation are commemorated by celebrating his birthday as National Education Day. Born in Mecca, then part of the Ottoman Empire (now Saudi Arabia), Azad’s family had origins in Herat. His father, Muhammad Khairuddin bin Ahmed Al Hussaini, was a Muslim scholar with thousands of disciples and claimed noble ancestry; his mother, Sheikha Alia bint Mohammad, was the daughter of Sheikh Mohammad bin Zaher AlWatri, a respected scholar from Medina. Azad settled in Calcutta with his family in 1890 and was home-schooled by family-appointed teachers. Fluent in Arabic, he mastered Bengali, Hindustani, Persian, and English, and was trained in the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali fiqh, Shariat, mathematics, philosophy, world history, and science. By age thirteen, he was married to Zulaikha Begum; by twelve, he wanted to write on Al-Ghazali; at fourteen, he contributed articles to Makhzan; at fifteen, he taught students older than him; and by sixteen, he completed the traditional curriculum nine years ahead of peers and launched a magazine. He began publishing a poetical journal, Nairang-e-Aalam, at age eleven and edited Al-Misbah by age twelve. In 1903, he launched Lissan-us-Sidq, which ran from December 1903 to May 1905 before closing due to funding issues. He joined Al-Nadwa in 1906 and edited Vakil from April 1906 to November 1906, later resuming the role until July 1908. In 1908, he traveled to Egypt, Syria, Turkey, and France, where he encountered revolutionaries like those of the Young Turk Movement and Iranian revolutionaries, which influenced his radical political views and led him to become a full-fledged Indian nationalist. He opposed British racial discrimination and Muslim communalism, rejecting the All-India Muslim League’s separatist stance. In 1905, he opposed the partition of Bengal and became active in revolutionary activities introduced by Aurobindo Ghosh and Shyam Sundar Chakravarty, organizing secret meetings in Bengal, Bihar, and Bombay. In 1912, he founded the Urdu weekly Al-Hilal in Calcutta, which openly criticized British policies and promoted Indian nationalism and Hindu-Muslim unity. Al-Hilal was banned in 1914 under the Press Act. In 1913, he became a founding member of the Anjuman-i-Ulama-i-Bangala, which later became the Jamiat Ulema-e-Bangala. He supported the Khilafat Movement to protect the Ottoman Sultan’s position as Caliph, which caused distress among Muslim conservatives. In 1916, he launched Al-Balagh, which was banned under the Defence of India Regulations Act, and was arrested; he was imprisoned in Ranchi until 1 January 1920. After release, he returned to a politically charged environment following the passage of the Rowlatt Acts in 1919 and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919. Gandhi, who had led successful non-violent revolts in Champaran and Kheda, organized the people and promoted Satyagraha. Azad and the Ali brothers welcomed Congress support for the Khilafat Movement and organized a non-cooperation campaign, including boycotts of British institutions and foreign goods. Azad joined the Congress and was elected president of the All India Khilafat Committee. He grew close to Gandhi and shared a deep passion for religion and non-violence (ahimsa), and developed friendships with Jawaharlal Nehru, Chittaranjan Das, and Subhas Chandra Bose. In 1921, he launched Paigham, which was banned by December 1921, and he and its editor, Abdul Razzak Mahilabadi, were arrested and sentenced to one year in prison. In 1922, the Khilafat and non-cooperation movements declined after violence at Chauri Chaura; Gandhi suspended the movement and fasted to repent. Despite this, Azad remained committed to Gandhi’s ideals. In 1923, at age 35, he became the youngest person to serve as President of the Indian National Congress. He led the Flag Satyagraha in Nagpur and presided over the 1924 Unity Conference in Delhi, which aimed to reunite Swarajists and Khilafat leaders under the Congress. He served on the Congress Working Committee and held positions as general secretary and president. In 1928, the Congress opposed the Simon Commission, which had no Indian members, and appointed the Motilal Nehru Commission to propose reforms. Azad endorsed the Nehru Report, which called for ending separate electorates and establishing a secular, independent India, and supported Gandhi’s call for dominion status within a year, or full independence otherwise. He aligned with Congress socialists like Nehru, Subhas Bose, and Jayaprakash Narayan and supported Nehru’s re-election in 1937. He advocated dialogue with Jinnah and the Muslim League between 1935 and 1937, rejecting the idea that the League represented only Muslims. In 1938, he mediated between Subhash Bose and Gandhi, standing by Gandhi and reluctantly supporting the Congress’s exit from provincial assemblies in 1939 after India’s entry into World War II without consultation. He criticized Jinnah for calling Congress rule “Hindu Raj” and the resignation of Congress ministries a “Day of Deliverance,” and opposed the Muslim League’s separatist agenda. At the 1940 Lahore session, when the League adopted a resolution for a separate Muslim state (Pakistan), Azad was elected Congress president in Ramgarh. In his presidential address, he strongly rejected the Two-Nation Theory, stating that Islam had a thousand-year claim on India and that all Hindus, Muslims, and Christians were Indians with equal pride in their religious identities.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, who served as Congress president from 1939 until 1946, strongly opposed the Muslim League's Two-Nation Theory and advocated for Hindu-Muslim unity, asserting that all Hindus and Muslims were Indians with shared bonds of brotherhood and nationhood. In his 1940 presidential address, he stated that Islam had a legitimate claim on Indian soil equal to Hinduism and that Indian Christians also had a rightful pride in being Indians. As the British faced growing unpopularity, Azad, along with Nehru and Gandhi, remained cautious about launching a full rebellion, fearing it would divide India and worsen the war situation. However, after intense debates in the Congress Working Committee in May and June 1942, Azad concluded that decisive action was necessary. He supported the "Quit India" call, traveled across India to rally support, and on 7 August 1942 inaugurated the struggle at Gowalia Tank in Mumbai. Two days later, he and the entire Congress leadership were arrested and imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort, where they remained under strict isolation and censorship for nearly four years. During imprisonment, Azad engaged in bridge, refereed tennis, taught Persian, Urdu, Indian and world history, and on 26 January each year commemorated the independence movement. He proposed negotiations with the British in 1943, arguing the rebellion had been mistimed, but the proposal was rejected. When Gandhi held talks with Jinnah in 1944, Azad criticized the move as counter-productive. After the war, the British agreed to transfer power, and all political prisoners were released in 1946. Azad led Congress in the elections for the Constituent Assembly and headed the delegation to negotiate with the British Cabinet Mission. He strongly supported the mission's 16 May proposal, which advocated a federal system with autonomy for provinces and grouping of provinces on religious lines—Group B for Muslim-majority West, Group C for Bengal and Assam, and Group A for the rest—arguing it would assuage Muslim concerns and bury Jinnah's demand for Pakistan. Despite opposition from Gandhi and others, the Working Committee approved the resolution with Azad and Patel's backing, and Azad secured Jinnah's agreement to the proposal. Azad resigned as Congress president in 1946, nominating Nehru, who led the interim government, and was appointed Minister of Education. He focused on rural education, girls' education, universal primary education, adult literacy, and vocational training, establishing the Central Institute of Education, the first Indian Institute of Technology in 1951, the University Grants Commission in 1953, and promoting the Indian Institute of Science and Delhi University's Faculty of Technology. He was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1952 from Rampur and won both Rampur and Gurgaon in 1957. Azad supported Nehru's socialist policies and social rights for women and underprivileged groups. He presided over the UNESCO General Conference in 1956 and wrote major works including India Wins Freedom, Ghubar-e-Khatir, and Tazkirah Tarjumanul Quran. Ghubar-e-Khatir, written between 1942 and 1946 during his imprisonment, consists of 24 letters to his friend Maulana Habibur Rahman Khan Sherwani, never sent due to restrictions, later published in 1946 by Ajmal Khan. The book covers complex topics like the existence of God, the origin of religions, and music in religion, with over 500 Persian and Arabic couplets. The book is seen as dealing with Azad’s social and spiritual life, while India Wins Freedom focuses on his political life. In 1989, the Ministry of Minority Affairs established the Maulana Azad Education Foundation and the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad National Fellowship to support minority students. In 1992, India posthumously awarded him the Bharat Ratna. Numerous institutions across India bear his name, including Maulana Azad Medical College, Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology, Maulana Azad National Urdu University, and the Maulana Azad Library at Aligarh Muslim University. His tomb, located next to Jama Masjid in Delhi, is a major national monument and receives many visitors; the Delhi High Court ordered its renovation in 2005. National Education Day is celebrated annually on 11 November, his birthday. Jawaharlal Nehru called him Mir-i-Karawan, and Gandhi described him as having the calibre of Plato, Aristotle, and Pythagoras. Azad was portrayed in the 1982 film Gandhi by Virendra Razdan, in a 1990s television series by Mangal Dhillon, in the docudrama Seher Hone Tak with Aamir Bashir, and in the 2019 film Woh Jo Tha Ek Massiah Maulana Azad with Linesh Fanse. Commemorative stamps were released by India Post.

The biographical film *Aashiq-e-Vatan* is about Maulana Azad, with the film *Woh Jo Tha Ek Massiah* released in 2019, directed by Rajendra Gupta Sanjay and Sanjay Singh Negi, and featuring Linesh Fanse in the lead role. Maulana Azad's birthday, 11 November, is observed as National Education Day in India. Commemorative stamps have been released by India Post, organized by year.
